what_happened: The job was a follow-up to the earlier speed-up of Athena's test check. The first reading chose cargo-nextest, pinned in athena.toml [tools], with a CI install step. The operator (the brain) then measured it. Nextest 0.9.148 ran the suite in 584 s against 673 s for cargo test, about 13% faster, which is not worth a new pinned tool. The operator replaced the approach: leave nextest out, and make the slowest test binaries faster (lifecycle 174 s, job_plan 83 s, drain 61 s, retry 54 s, steward 48 s) without removing or weakening any test. The operator also set a target of under 6 minutes for the full run and asked for before and after per-binary times in docs/decisions.md, with nextest recorded as a rejected alternative. The reading did not match what the user meant.
cause: The speed-up lever was picked from an earlier operator correction and never tested against measurements. The earlier correction named nextest as the lever, and the next reading adopted it without a step that measures the gain from a candidate tool, or that profiles each test binary, before the method is fixed. Nothing in the system requires a speed-up reading to state its expected gain with a measurement. That left the operator to run the comparison by hand and rewrite the approach a second time.
prevention: Add a required measurement step to any request or reading whose goal is speed. Before the reading fixes a method, it must record a per-stage or per-binary timeline from a real run. It must also try each candidate lever, such as a different test runner, and record the measured gain next to a minimum worthwhile threshold. The reading may add a new pinned tool only if the measured gain clears that threshold. Otherwise it must target the largest time consumers directly. The reading must also carry the target time and require the before and after numbers, with rejected alternatives, in docs/decisions.md. A check should refuse a speed reading that has no measured baseline.
proposed_request: Speed up Athena's full test run without removing or weakening any test. Do not adopt cargo-nextest: on this 4-core machine it ran the suite in 584 s against 673 s for cargo test, about 13% faster, which is not worth a new pinned tool or CI install step. Instead, time each slow athena-cli test binary individually: tests/lifecycle.rs (174 s), tests/job_plan.rs (83 s), tests/drain.rs (61 s), tests/retry.rs (54 s) and tests/steward.rs (48 s). Find where the time goes, for example real sleeps, poll intervals, deadlines, repeated repository setup or serial locks. Then cut it with shorter test-only intervals, shared fixtures built once, and less needless real git or process work. Target: the full `cargo test --locked` finishes in under 6 minutes on this machine. Acceptance: (1) every existing test is still present and still asserts what it did before; (2) the full `cargo test --locked` passes and its measured time is under 6 minutes; (3) docs/decisions.md has a decision entry with the before and after time for each of the five binaries, measured in the job, and the nextest measurement (584 s against 673 s) recorded as a rejected alternative; (4) athena.toml [tools], CI and the producer guidance gain no new tool.
